copious

/KO-pee-us/ — stress on KO · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Copious describes something that exists in large, plentiful amounts, more than enough.

Copious rain in April left the reservoirs full for the first time in years.

Example

The university library received copious donations of rare manuscripts after the estate sale.

Copi (plenty, from Latin copia) + -ous (full of) = full of plenty. The library didn't just receive a few manuscripts or even a standard collection — copious means an overflowing, abundant quantity that's almost overwhelming. This is a more-than-enough abundance.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

profuse: Profuse describes something pouring out freely — profuse apologies, profuse sweat, a profuse nosebleed. It suits things that gush in the moment. Copious is about sheer accumulated quantity: copious rainfall, copious evidence, a copious supply. If it streams out of someone, call it profuse; if it piles up far past what is needed, call it copious.

lavish: Lavish means given or spent with generous, even showy extravagance — a lavish party, lavish praise. It points at the giver's open hand. Copious measures only amount: a copious supply is simply enormous, whether or not anyone was being generous. Rain can be copious, but only a host can be lavish.

ample: Ample means generously sufficient — an ample budget covers each need with money left over, and ample legroom lets you stretch out. It stops at comfortably enough. Copious races past that mark: a copious stack of firewood buries the whole porch. Ample promises you will not run short; copious suggests you may run out of room.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sparse: thinly scattered; present in small amounts

meager: barely enough; deficient in quantity

Where it sits · how far past what is needed — enough → plentiful → abundant → copious

enough vs. copious: Enough food feeds everyone once, but copious food leaves the platters overflowing.

plentiful vs. copious: A plentiful harvest fills the barn; a copious harvest spills out of it.

abundant vs. copious: Abundant rain soaks the fields, but copious rain fills every reservoir to the brim.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — copi

Root — copi: plenty, abundance — from Latin copia; never became a standalone English word (Latin (copia))

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of (Latin (-osus))

Put it together

Put it together: The base copi- never became an independent English word; it comes from Latin copia, 'plenty.' Add -ous ('full of') and copious means 'full of plenty' — existing in overflowing, more-than-generous amounts.

Use the root in a new word: cornucopia

Use the root in a new word: cornucopia: The farmers' market was a cornucopia of fresh fruits, cheeses, and warm baked goods.

Word Choice

formal

Reach for copious when you want to emphasize an overflowing, generous amount—more than enough, and often impressive. Use it for copious evidence, copious rainfall, copious notes. It has a somewhat formal tone, so it's more at home in academic or professional writing than in casual conversation.
